elements.id-string-3: We present frequency-matched strobo-spectroscopy (FMSS) of charge migration (CM) in bromodiacetylene, simulated with time-dependent density-functional theory.
elements.id-string-4: CM+FMSS is a pump-probe scheme that uses a frequency-matched HHG-driving laser as an independent probe step following the creation of a localized hole on the bromine atom that induces CM dynamics.
elements.id-string-5: We show that the delay-dependent harmonic yield tracks the phase of the CM dynamics through its sensitivity to the amount of electron density on the bromine end of the molecule.
elements.id-string-6: FMSS takes advantage of the intrinsic attosecond time resolution of the HHG process, in which different harmonics are emitted at different times and thus probe different locations of the electron hole.
elements.id-string-7: Finally, we show that the CM-induced modulation of the HHG signal is dominated by the recombination step of the HHG process, with negligible contribution from the ionization step.
elements.id-string-9: Understanding the ultrafast motion of electrons within matter is of critical importance for many areas of science and technology.
elements.id-string-10: One example is charge migration \cite{calegari2016, worner2017, nisoli2017, li2020} (CM): the coherent motion of a positively-charged electron hole along the backbone of a molecule following a localized ionization event, which can be observed on Angstrom spatial scales and attosecond time scales \cite{goulielmakis2010, calegari2014, kraus2015}.
elements.id-string-11: CM is a widely-studied phenomenon due to its potential for understanding and perhaps steering downstream processes such as chemical reactions, photosynthesis, and photovoltaics via charge-directed reactivity \cite{remacle1998, golubev2015, mauger2022}.
elements.id-string-12: Since its discovery in the late 1990s \cite{cederbaum1999, breidbach2003}, the study of CM has flourished \cite{lunnemann2008, golubev2015, kuleff2016, bruner2017, folorunso2021, mansson2021}, with much of this research performed in recent years \cite{barillot2022, li2022, schlegel2022, yong2022, zhao2022, folorunso2023, yu2023, he2022, hamer2022, matselyukh2022, kobayashi2022}.
elements.id-string-13: Despite the many challenges of doing experiments on the attosecond timescale, CM has been measured using several different techniques, including X-ray absorption spectroscopy \cite{bressler2010, goulielmakis2010, kobayashi2022, matselyukh2022}, photoelectron spectroscopy \cite{bandrauk2004, stolow2004, calegari2014, ayuso2017, lara-astiaso2018}, and high-harmonic spectroscopy (HHS) \cite{bredtmann2012, worner2013, kraus2015, peng2019, he2022}.
elements.id-string-14: Due to its inherent sub-femtosecond temporal resolution via the attochirp \cite{dudovich2006, smirnova2009, azoury2017} of the harmonic radiation, in which different harmonic energies are emitted at different times during the laser cycle, HHS is particularly well-suited to perform time-resolved measurements of ultrafast electron dynamics via a pump-probe scheme.

elements.id-string-278: We present frequency-matched strobo-spectroscopy (FMSS) of charge migration (CM) in bromobutadiyne, simulated with time-dependent density-functional theory.
elements.id-string-279: Since its discovery in the late 1990s \cite{cederbaum1999, breidbach2003}, the study of CM has flourished \cite{lunnemann2008, bredtmann2012, golubev2015, kuleff2016, bruner2017, folorunso2021, mansson2021}, with much of this research performed in recent years \cite{barillot2022, li2022, schlegel2023, yong2022, zhao2022, folorunso2023, yu2023, he2022, hamer2022, matselyukh2022, kobayashi2022, he2023}.
elements.id-string-280: Despite the many challenges of doing experiments on the attosecond timescale, CM has been measured using several different techniques, including X-ray absorption spectroscopy \cite{goulielmakis2010, matselyukh2022, barillot2022, young2018}, photoelectron spectroscopy \cite{stolow2004, calegari2014, ayuso2017, lara-astiaso2018}, and high-harmonic spectroscopy (HHS) \cite{worner2013, kraus2015, peng2019, he2022}.
elements.id-string-281: Due to its inherent sub-femtosecond temporal resolution via the attochirp \cite{mairesse2003, dudovich2006, smirnova2009, azoury2017} of the harmonic radiation, in which different harmonic energies are emitted at different times during the laser cycle, HHS is particularly well-suited to perform time-resolved measurements of ultrafast electron dynamics via a pump-probe scheme.
elements.id-string-282: It is useful make a distinction between schemes where the CM is initiated by the same laser field that probes those dynamics, in which the CM dynamics is re-initiated every half-laser cycle~\cite{kraus2015, he2022, he2023}, and schemes where the pump and probe steps are independent \cite{hamer2022}, as discussed here.
elements.id-string-283: We induce CM dynamics in a bromobutadiyne (BrC$_{4}$H) molecule via the creation of a localized hole on the bromine end of the molecule \cite{folorunso2021, hamer2022}.
elements.id-string-284: In our recent work~\cite{hamer2022}, we showed that the CM frequency can be extracted using a different application of HHS, based on creating sidebands in the harmonic spectrum for a broad range of laser frequencies not commensurate with the CM frequency.
elements.id-string-285: In the current manuscript, FMSS allows us to go further and perform a time- and space-resolved analysis of the CM dynamics by exploiting the intrinsic time dependence of the HHG process (the attochirp).
elements.id-string-286: \includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth]{Figures/figure1.png}\caption{Schematic of our CM+FMSS analysis: (a) snapshots of the time-dependent CM dynamics following the creation of a localized hole on the bromine atom for two different time delays (purple and green frames).
elements.id-string-287: (c) The resulting orbital-resolved, normalized CM+FMSS spectrum (see text) over half an optical cycle for delays near 4.50 optical cycles (approximately $18\, \text{fs}$ after the initiation of the CM).
elements.id-string-288: In Figure~{\ref{fig:1}}, we show a schematic which describes the FMSS concept: panel (a) depicts the time-dependent CM dynamics at two different time delays after initiation (purple and green frames, respectively).
elements.id-string-289: In our CM+FMSS simulations, we start by creating a one-electron valence hole localized on the halogen end of a bromobutadiyne ($\text{BrC}_{4}\text{H}$) molecule.
elements.id-string-290: Our preliminary modeling of how to initiate this type of localized CM using a realistic pump pulse is encouraging: we find that both attosecond XUV pulses and few-femtosecond intense infrared pulses initiate similar modes of CM as those discussed in this paper, although we have yet to implement a full calculation including both a realistic pump along with the FMSS-driving pulse.
elements.id-string-291: In all TDDFT calculations shown in this paper, nuclear dynamics have been omitted.
elements.id-string-292: The oscillating charge density along the molecular axis induces a significant dipole contribution along the axis of the molecular backbone, as was also observed in Kuleff \emph{et al}~\cite{kuleff2011}.
elements.id-string-293: However, above 20 eV, the total emission spectrum is dominated by the driven (harmonic) response, with the CM-only emission rapidly decreasing with respect to the emission frequency.
elements.id-string-294: Below the cutoff energy $E_{c} = 40\ \text{eV}$, this spectral maximum trends towards earlier delays as the harmonic frequency increases.
elements.id-string-295: Removing the attochirp from our model calculations (first term in Eq.~{\ref{eq:model_phase}}) eliminates the slope of the variation shown in Fig.~{\ref{fig:3}}(b), since in the absence of the attochirp all electron trajectories return at the same time regardless of harmonic frequency.
elements.id-string-296: We also note that the time resolution built into FMSS via the attochirp means that there will be a delay and frequency dependence to the harmonic yield even if $\omega_{CM}$ does not match $\omega_{L}/2$ exactly, {\it i.e.}, as long as $1/|\omega_{CM}-\omega_{L}/2|$ is small compared to the time (delay) duration over which the CM is sampled.
elements.id-string-297: This is a crucial result: because there is a spatially-resolvable feature in the harmonic spectrum -- here, a decrease in the harmonic yield when the hole is located on the halogen atom -- we are able to perform a time- and space-resolved analysis of the CM dynamics using FMSS.
elements.id-string-298: By exploiting a site-specific feature of the HHG spectrum, we achieve a time- and space-resolved analysis of the CM by performing a sub-cycle-resolved delay scan.
elements.id-string-299: It is interesting to consider how the FMSS envisioned in this paper would fare when considering more realistic experimental conditions, in particular the two approximations we are making concerning (i) the (perfect) perpendicular alignment of the molecule relative to the laser polarization, and (ii) the absence of nuclear motion.
elements.id-string-300: For (i), we expect the biggest issue to be that a laser field component that is parallel to the molecular backbone will drive CM that is not necessarily in phase with the field-free CM, and which will therefore likely give rise to a different delay dependence.
elements.id-string-301: For bromobutadiyne interacting with the few-cycle laser pulse we have used here, we find that the harmonic response to a parallel-polarized laser pulse does indeed exhibit a different delay dependence but that it is also substantially weaker than that of the perpendicular-polarized pulse and thus does not contribute much in the total delay dependence.
elements.id-string-302: For the longer driving pulses used in Ref.\cite{hamer2022}, we found that the sideband-based HHS proposed in that paper was valid for a full-width half-maximum angular distribution of 40$^{\circ}$.
elements.id-string-303: Given the weaker response for the shorter pulse duration used here, we expect that FMSS will also tolerate at least 40$^{\circ}$ of angular distribution.
elements.id-string-304: For (ii) we can estimate the effect of including nuclear motion in several different ways.
elements.id-string-305: First, we have performed preliminary calculations of CM in bromobutadiyne when including Ehrenfest dynamics and find  that the molecule is quite rigid.
elements.id-string-306: A complete characterization of the effect of nuclear motion,  scanning over initial geometries as well as the sub-cycle-resolved delay, is currently computationally intractable when also calculating the HHG spectrum.
elements.id-string-307: However, it is also useful to think about the time scale for the nuclear dynamics compared to that of the short pulse and few cycles of probing that we discuss here.
elements.id-string-308: In particular, by incorporating decoherence into the model calculations described above we find that FMSS remains applicable within the typical time scale for nuclear dynamics and decoherence.
elements.id-string-309: Given the intense, current interest in probing and understanding charge migration, with a range of experiments underway at large-scale X-ray facilities\cite{li2022, grell2023}, approaches based on HHS, such as FMSS, could be appealing due to the much wider availability of table-top based HHG sources.
